concepts.name: Article 356: Constitutional Basis and Textual Provisions
key_dimensions: Exact constitutional language — 'government of the state cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution'
Two triggering mechanisms: Governor's report vs. President acting 'otherwise' (without Governor's report)
UPSC trap: President can act even WITHOUT Governor's report — 'otherwise than on report' clause
Comparison with Article 355 as a precondition/duty that justifies Article 356 invocation

concepts.name: Article 355: Union's Duty to States — The Gateway to Article 356
key_dimensions: Twin duties: protect states from external aggression AND internal disturbance; ensure governance as per Constitution
UPSC trap: Article 355 is a standalone duty, not merely a preamble to Article 356
SR Bommai case used Article 355 as a check — Centre must first exhaust Article 355 remedies
Difference between 'internal disturbance' (Art. 355) vs. 'armed rebellion' (Art. 352) — 44th Amendment significance

concepts.name: Article 365: Failure to Comply with Union Directions
key_dimensions: Exact provision: if a state fails to comply with Union directions under the Constitution, it shall be lawful for the President to hold that Article 356 situation has arisen
UPSC trap: Article 365 does NOT itself impose President's Rule — it only creates a LEGAL PRESUMPTION that enables Article 356
Link to Articles 256, 257 (Union directions to states) — compliance with which is enforced via Art. 365
Difference from Article 356: Art. 356 requires breakdown of constitutional machinery; Art. 365 provides a route based on deliberate non-compliance

concepts.name: Proclamation under Article 356: Parliamentary Approval Requirements
key_dimensions: Must be approved by BOTH Houses within 2 months by simple majority — UPSC trap: NOT special majority
If Lok Sabha is dissolved before approval, proclamation survives until 30 days after new Lok Sabha's first sitting, provided Rajya Sabha has approved
Duration: initially 6 months, extendable up to 3 years with parliamentary approval every 6 months
Beyond 1 year: requires both (i) national emergency to be in operation OR (ii) Election Commission certification that elections cannot be held

concepts.name: Effects of Proclamation under Article 356 on State Executive and Legislature
key_dimensions: President assumes functions of State Government; Governor acts as President's agent
State Legislature's powers exercised by Parliament — Parliament can delegate to President
UPSC trap: High Court's constitutional position is NOT affected — HC continues to function independently
State Legislature may be suspended (not necessarily dissolved) — President can dissolve ONLY after Lok Sabha approval or if Lok Sabha itself is dissolved

concepts.name: Revocation and Expiry of Article 356 Proclamation
key_dimensions: President can revoke the proclamation at any time WITHOUT parliamentary approval — UPSC trap
Automatic expiry if not approved/extended by Parliament
SR Bommai ruling: Courts can review whether revocation was proper; reinstatement of dismissed government possible
Post-revocation restoration of state legislature — legislative acts passed during President's Rule remain valid

concepts.name: SR Bommai Case (1994): Landmark Judicial Curtailment of Article 356
key_dimensions: Nine-judge bench: Article 356 is justiciable — mala fide or irrelevant grounds make proclamation unconstitutional
Floor test doctrine: majority of government must be tested on the floor of the House, not assessed by Governor in private
UPSC trap: Court CANNOT restore dismissed government during pendency of case (but can after quashing)
Secularism as a basic feature — anti-secular activities of a state government can justify Art. 356 invocation

concepts.name: Governor's Role and the Potential for Misuse of Article 356
key_dimensions: Governor's report is the primary trigger but is NOT binding — President can act 'otherwise'
Sarkaria Commission finding: Governor should be a 'constitutional sentinel,' not an agent of the Centre
UPSC trap: Governor's report is NOT available as a right to the state — confidentiality vs. transparency tension post-SR Bommai
Punchhi Commission recommendation: Governor's report should be placed before Parliament along with the proclamation

concepts.name: Sarkaria Commission Recommendations on Article 356
key_dimensions: Article 356 should be used as a 'last resort' — sparingly and only after exhausting Article 355
Warning to errant state before invoking 356 (except in extreme urgency)
UPSC trap: Sarkaria Commission did NOT recommend abolition of Article 356 — it recommended strict safeguards
Recommendation that the proclamation be subject to judicial review — later upheld in SR Bommai

concepts.name: Punchhi Commission (2010) Recommendations on Article 356
key_dimensions: Recommended localised emergency — Centre should be able to act in specific areas of a state, not necessarily take over the entire state
Suggested a 'sunset clause' for Article 356 proclamations — limited initial duration with strict renewal
UPSC trap: Punchhi Commission was MORE recent than Sarkaria (2010 vs. 1988) and had additional federal perspective
Recommended deletion of the words 'or otherwise' from Article 356 to prevent misuse

concepts.name: Comparison: Article 356 vs. Article 352 (National Emergency)
key_dimensions: Article 352: external aggression/armed rebellion; Art. 356: constitutional breakdown in a state — different triggers
UPSC trap: Under Art. 352, State Legislature continues to function; under Art. 356, state legislature is suspended/dissolved
Approval majority: Art. 352 requires special majority (2/3 + majority of total membership); Art. 356 requires only SIMPLE majority
Art. 352 affects Centre-State relations broadly; Art. 356 is state-specific

concepts.name: Legislative Competence During President's Rule: Article 357
key_dimensions: Parliament can confer power on President to legislate on state subjects during President's Rule
Parliament can delegate this legislative power further to any authority specified by President
UPSC trap: Laws made by Parliament under Art. 357 during President's Rule DO NOT automatically lapse when President's Rule ends — they continue until repealed by competent legislature
Distinction between laws made under Art. 356 (by Parliament directly) vs. laws made under Art. 357 (delegated to President)

concepts.name: Misuse and Political History of Article 356
key_dimensions: Used over 125 times since 1950 — most notoriously during Indira Gandhi era (UPSC context: 1975-77 period)
Famous cases: dismissal of E.M.S. Namboodiripad's Kerala government (1959 — first ever use), Arunachal Pradesh (2016) quashed by Supreme Court
UPSC trap: The Arunachal Pradesh case (Nabam Rebia, 2016) reinforced that Governor cannot unilaterally advance Assembly session to facilitate floor test leading to Art. 356
Political misuse led to 44th Amendment proposals (not fully implemented regarding Art. 356)

concepts.name: 44th Constitutional Amendment Act (1978) and Article 356
key_dimensions: 44th Amendment changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion' in Art. 352 but did NOT similarly tighten Art. 356 — UPSC trap
Proposed that Art. 356 proclamation be approved by special majority — this provision was NOT enacted (only proposed)
Added safeguard: Rajya Sabha must approve if Lok Sabha is dissolved before approval of proclamation
Context: reaction to Emergency (1975-77) abuses — shows political will vs. actual constitutional change gap

concepts.name: Article 356 and the Basic Structure Doctrine
key_dimensions: SR Bommai: federalism is a basic feature — Art. 356 cannot be used to destroy the federal character of the Constitution
UPSC trap: Art. 356 itself is NOT unconstitutional as it exists in the Constitution, but its MISUSE can be struck down
Parliamentary democracy at state level is also a basic feature — dissolution of legislature requires stricter scrutiny
Tension between parliamentary sovereignty (approving proclamation) and judicial review of the same

concepts.name: Union Directions to States: Articles 256 and 257 — Precondition for Article 365
key_dimensions: Art. 256: States must exercise executive power to ensure compliance with laws of Parliament
Art. 257: States must not impede Union's executive power; Union can give directions regarding construction/maintenance of means of communication declared to be of national/military importance
UPSC trap: Failure under Art. 256/257 triggers Art. 365 legal presumption, NOT automatic President's Rule
Art. 257A (inserted by 42nd Amendment, repealed by 44th Amendment): allowed Centre to deploy armed forces in states — its repeal is significant

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Article 356 Proclamation: Scope and Limits
key_dimensions: SR Bommai: Courts CAN examine whether the material before President was relevant and non-mala fide
UPSC trap: Courts review the EXISTENCE and RELEVANCE of material, NOT its SUFFICIENCY — doctrine of limited judicial review
Remedy: Court can quash proclamation and restore the state government; Parliament's approval does NOT immunize proclamation from judicial review
Cabinet's advice to President under Art. 74 is not justiciable, but the FACTUAL BASIS of advice can be examined

concepts.name: Role of Rajya Sabha in Safeguarding States under Article 356
key_dimensions: Rajya Sabha as the 'Council of States' — its approval is MANDATORY for extension beyond 6 months
UPSC trap: Unlike Art. 352 where joint sitting is possible, Art. 356 proclamation requires SEPARATE approval of each House — no joint sitting provision
If Lok Sabha passes a resolution disapproving the proclamation, President must revoke it — Rajya Sabha alone cannot save it after Lok Sabha disapproval
Historical significance: Rajya Sabha has occasionally acted as a check when ruling party didn't have majority there

concepts.name: Centre-State Relations during President's Rule: Financial Implications
key_dimensions: State's Consolidated Fund continues to exist — but Parliament can authorise expenditure from it
UPSC trap: Finance Commission awards and grants-in-aid continue; President's Rule does NOT suspend financial federalism automatically
Parliament can impose taxes that state legislature could have imposed — temporary but significant fiscal centralisation
Post-President's Rule: financial accountability and audit of expenditure made during the period — CAG's role

concepts.name: Article 356 in Coalition Era and Contemporary Relevance
key_dimensions: Post-SR Bommai (1994), usage has significantly declined — judicial deterrence effect
Recent controversies: Uttarakhand (2016), Arunachal Pradesh (2016) — both proclamations quashed by courts
UPSC relevance: Governors' discretionary powers and partisan behaviour remain contested — Nabam Rebia case guidelines
Debate on abolition vs. retention with stricter safeguards — reflects tension between unity and diversity in Indian federalism
